law: You can use this framework to import and export assets from and to a variety of industry standard file formats supported by popular authoring tools and game engines.
You can also use Model I/O to generate or process model and texture data—for example, to create subdivision surfaces, to bake ambient occlusion textures, or to generate light probes.
Use the class to load these objects from a file or to create a collection of 3D objects for export to a file.
Use the class to inspect or rearrange a mesh’s vertex and index data format.
Use classes that adopt the and protocols to minimize the number of times a mesh’s vertex and index data is copied and translated between loading, processing, and rendering on a GPU.
Use methods (for example, the method) to process a model, generating additional data—such as surface normals, tangent basis vectors, ambient occlusion, or light maps—for use in rendering.
Use the class and its subclasses to generate procedural textures such as noise, normal maps, and realistic sky boxes.
Use the class to generate light sources whose illumination is based on the contents of a scene.
Use the class to work with a volumetric description of a model.
The and classes describe realistic lighting properties for use in rendering, and the class also supports physically based rendering parameters.
Like other procedural subclasses, the class generates texel data only when that data is first referenced, and then caches it for future use.
After you first create a sky cube texture, Model I/O does not generate texture data until you use one of the methods listed inAccessing Texture Data.
You use the class or one of its subclasses to identify, load, or create texture data, and then associate textures with materials using the and classes.
